description: A deep album cut from Burning Spear's Appointment With His Majesty (1997), written and arranged by Winston Rodney himself. Roots reggae at its most unhurried — a veteran artist singing about the music that carried him.

pops.text: Deep cut alert: 'Music' is track 11 on Appointment With His Majesty, the 1997 album by Jamaican roots legend Burning Spear.
Burning Spear is Winston Rodney, born March 1, 1945, in Saint Ann's Bay, Jamaica — the same parish as Bob Marley and Marcus Garvey.
Every song on this album was written and arranged by Rodney himself. No outside writers, no shortcuts — pure Spear.
The name Burning Spear came from Jomo Kenyatta, Kenya's first president, whose nickname it was before Rodney took it as his own.
Career tip of the century: in 1969 Bob Marley advised Rodney to try Coxsone Dodd's Studio One — where his first single, 'Door Peep,' was born.
At 4 minutes 54 seconds, 'Music' gets room to breathe. Roots reggae rarely hurries, and neither does he.
AllMusic noted this album found Rodney experimenting with a distinctly folky sound alongside his usual deep roots groove.
Appointment With His Majesty peaked at No. 10 on Billboard's Reggae Albums chart — three decades into his recording career.
The album was nominated for Best Reggae Album at the 40th Grammy Awards in 1998. Spear would finally win the trophy in 2000, for Calling Rastafari.
His defining album remains 1975's Marcus Garvey, a salute to the Jamaican hero. 'Music' is that same mission, 22 years on.

title: Music

artist: Charles Wright & The Watts 103rd Street Rhythm Band
description: Not the Steve Miller song — this 'Joker' is a horn-driven 1969 funk instrumental from In the Jungle, Babe, full title 'The Joker (On a Trip Thru the Jungle).' A dancefloor stomper from L.A.'s Watts 103rd Street Rhythm Band.

pops.text: Wrong Joker! This is not Steve Miller's 1973 hit — it's a 1969 funk instrumental, full title 'The Joker (On a Trip Thru the Jungle).'
The track comes from In the Jungle, Babe, recorded in June 1969 at Western Recorders in Hollywood, California.
Songwriting credit goes to Miles Grayson. Charles Wright produced it, with arrangements by Al McKay and Bill Cannon.
One reviewer called it 'a furious, horn-driven dancefloor stomper with twanging guitar.' Hard to argue — just listen.
The band had form with instrumentals — as the Soul Runners they'd already scored in 1967 with 'Grits and Cornbread' and 'Spreadin' Honey.'
An earlier live 'Joker' was taped May 18, 1968, at Hollywood's Haunted House nightclub, and finally released decades later on Live at the Haunted House.
Guitarist Al McKay left the Watts band in 1969 and soon joined Earth, Wind & Fire. That guitar chair had serious alumni energy.
The Watts band backed comedian Bill Cosby in the studio, an association that helped land them a Warner Bros. deal — the label's first R&B signing.
Its parent album also held the soulful hit 'Love Land' plus covers of the Doors' 'Light My Fire' and Sly Stone's 'Everyday People.'
Afterlife: this 1969 Warner recording later resurfaced on After Hours: The Collection — Northern Soul Masters, finding a new dancefloor audience.

title: The Joker

artist: Charles Wright & The Watts 103rd Street Rhythm Band
description: Charles Wright's 1970 signature song — a sunny, self-empowering funk anthem he had to sneak into the studio to record. It hit No. 12 pop and No. 3 R&B, then lived a second life through N.W.A and countless samples.

pops.text: The title was born on stage: performing 'Do Your Thing' at Texas A&M, Wright kept urging the crowd to express themselves — and a song title stuck.
Nobody wanted to record it, so Wright snuck a bass player, drummer and engineer into the studio one Sunday and cut it in secret.
Warner Bros.' president told Wright he'd made a mistake, and so did every DJ he played it for. Wright kept his feeling it was a hit.
He was right: released in August 1970, it reached No. 12 on the Billboard Hot 100 and No. 3 on the R&B chart.
That groove is Melvin Dunlap on bass and James Gadson on drums — a rhythm section that later backed Bill Withers on Still Bill.
Try singing the tongue-twister once: 'It's not what you look like when you're doin' what you're doin'...' Three times fast? Forget it.
The single was nominated for a 1971 Grammy for Best R&B Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocals, losing to the Delfonics.
Surprise: it wasn't even their biggest chart hit — 'Do Your Thing' peaked one notch higher, at No. 11, in 1969.
N.W.A sampled it for their own 'Express Yourself' on Straight Outta Compton. Wright heard it, called Ice Cube, got an apology — and his royalties.
The afterlife kept rolling: Labrinth sampled it in 2012, Tyler, the Creator sampled the N.W.A version in 2017, and it powers the climax of Mr. & Mrs. Smith.

title: Express Yourself

description: The Commodores' 1985 tribute to Marvin Gaye and Jackie Wilson, who both died in 1984, imagining them still singing on heaven's night shift. It hit No. 3 in the US and won the group their first Grammy.

pops.text: This is a eulogy you can dance to: a tribute to Marvin Gaye and Jackie Wilson, two soul giants who both died in 1984.
Drummer Walter Orange began writing it after their deaths. Producer Dennis Lambert added the music, and Franne Golde came up with the title.
Listen for the hidden quotes: the Marvin verse borrows from Gaye's own 'What's Going On' — 'talk to me, so you can see what's going on.'
The Jackie verse is just as coded: 'working out' nods to Wilson's 1963 hit 'Baby Workout,' and 'lifted us higher and higher' to his signature song.
Jackie Wilson, nicknamed 'Mr. Excitement,' had collapsed on stage in 1975 and spent years in a coma before his death in January 1984.
Marvin Gaye was shot by his own father in April 1984, just three months after Wilson's death. The grief in this song was fresh.
Comeback story: this was the Commodores' first hit with new co-lead singer J.D. Nicholas, formerly of Heatwave, after Lionel Richie's departure.
Chart run: No. 1 on the R&B chart for four weeks and No. 3 on the Billboard Hot 100 — a tribute song as a genuine smash.
In 1986 it won the Commodores their first Grammy, for Best R&B Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocals.
In 2010 the group re-recorded it in tribute to Michael Jackson, and in 2022 Bruce Springsteen covered it on Only the Strong Survive.

title: Nightshift

description: Lionel Richie's gentle 1977 breakup ballad for the Commodores — famously, the narrator isn't heartbroken, he's 'easy like Sunday morning.' It topped the R&B chart, reached No. 4 pop, and reshaped the group's sound.

pops.text: A breakup song with no tears: Lionel Richie wrote it about a man who feels relief, not heartbreak, as a relationship ends.
Richie aimed for another crossover hit after 'Just to Be Close to You' had topped the R&B chart and hit No. 7 pop in 1976.
Released in March 1977 as a single from the group's fifth, self-titled album on Motown.
Chart verdict: No. 1 on Billboard's Hot Soul Singles chart for a week in July 1977, and No. 4 on the Hot 100.
Across the Atlantic it reached No. 9 in both the UK and New Zealand — a Sunday morning that travelled well.
Musicians, take note: it's written in A-flat major, then the album version modulates up a semitone to A major for the repeated choruses.
Its success paved the way for more Richie ballads — 'Three Times a Lady' and 'Still' soon made slow songs the Commodores' signature.
Most unlikely cover: Faith No More recorded it during the Angel Dust sessions, after playing it live in place of Black Sabbath's 'War Pigs.'
Faith No More dropped the second verse, yet took it to No. 1 in Australia and No. 3 in the UK — their highest-charting UK hit.
Richie revisited it himself in 2012 on Tuskegee, duetting with Willie Nelson — country-soul, full circle.

title: Easy

description: John Fogerty's farewell heartbreaker from Mardi Gras, Creedence's final album. A boy asks his departing father why, gets told 'someday you'll understand,' and grows up to learn the hardest lesson in the catalog: someday never comes.

pops.text: Released in May 1972, this was Creedence Clearwater Revival's final single. The band officially broke up that October.
It peaked at No. 25 on the Billboard Hot 100 in June 1972. Modest for CCR, who famously racked up five No. 2 hits without ever reaching No. 1.
The B-side was 'Tearin' Up the Country,' written and sung by drummer Doug Clifford. Even the flip side belonged to somebody else by then.
Fogerty said the song grew out of his parents' divorce: as a boy he was told, 'Someday, you'll understand.' His verdict as a grown man: 'The truth is that you never do.'
The painful twist: Fogerty wrote it while his own marriage was ending, catching himself telling his own kids the same empty 'someday' line.
Brother Tom Fogerty had already quit, so Mardi Gras was a trio album where Stu Cook and Doug Clifford wrote and sang their own songs for the first time.
Fogerty later wrote that the band's turmoil robbed this song of the power and complexity he had envisioned for its arrangement. He heard a bigger record than CCR could still make.
Critics were brutal to Mardi Gras — Rolling Stone's Jon Landau called it the worst album he had ever heard from a major rock band. This track was the consensus keeper.
Mardi Gras was Creedence's seventh studio album in under four years. Seven albums, a stack of hits, and gone — one of rock's fastest rises and falls.
The song earned its afterlife on Chronicle, CCR's greatest-hits collection, where it sits alongside 'Proud Mary' and 'Fortunate Son' as essential Creedence.

title: Someday Never Comes

description: The candle-in-the-window closer of Cosmo's Factory. Released as the flip side of 'Lookin' Out My Back Door,' Fogerty's soulful pledge to find his way home became a double-sided No. 2 hit and a staple of his solo years.

pops.text: This is the closing track of Cosmo's Factory, released in July 1970. After all that swamp-rock muscle, CCR ended their biggest album with a slow-burning prayer.
It was the flip side of 'Lookin' Out My Back Door,' and the double-sided single peaked at No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100. A B-side with A-side numbers.
In the UK the sides were flipped: 'Long As I Can See The Light' was the A-side and reached No. 20. It went all the way to No. 1 in Norway.
That soulful tenor sax solo? That's John Fogerty himself. He also played the electric piano — singer, guitarist, writer, producer, and now horn section.
Cosmo's Factory spent nine weeks at No. 1 in America. It was CCR's fifth album in two years, a pace that looks superhuman now.
Creedence never played this song live. Fogerty finally performed it on his Blue Moon Swamp tour, opening at San Francisco's Fillmore on May 18, 1997 — 27 years later.
Listen to the drum beat: Moby sampled it for 'The Sky Is Broken' on his 1999 blockbuster Play. CCR's groove quietly powered an electronica hit.
Fogerty re-recorded the song with My Morning Jacket at Nashville's Blackbird Studio for his 2013 duets album Wrote a Song for Everyone.
In 2020, Craft Recordings released a fan-generated video for the song ahead of Father's Day, built from fans' clips of their fathers and grandfathers — their own guiding lights.
Fogerty revisited it again for 2025's Legacy: The Creedence Clearwater Revival Years, re-recording his CCR classics with his sons Shane and Tyler — after finally regaining ownership of his catalog.

title: Long As I Can See The Light

description: A post-nuclear escape fantasy written aboard David Crosby's boat by Crosby, Stephen Stills and Jefferson Airplane's Paul Kantner. Both bands recorded it in 1969; this is the CSN debut-album version, all eerie calm and silver people.

pops.text: Written in 1968 in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, aboard Crosby's schooner Mayan. Naturally, a song about escaping by boat started on an actual boat.
The division of labor: Crosby composed the music, while Paul Kantner and Stephen Stills wrote most of the lyrics. Three writers, two bands, one song.
The premise is pure science fiction: the writers imagined themselves as survivors of a nuclear war, escaping by sea to start a new civilization.
Those 'silver people on the shoreline'? Crosby explained they were guys in radiation suits. The politest possible request follows: 'let us be.'
The 'purple berries' in the lyric have been explained as iodine pills against radiation, and the ships are wooden because metal could turn radioactive. Details, details.
Kantner got no credit on the original 1969 CSN release. He was feuding with Jefferson Airplane's manager Matthew Katz, who might have slapped an injunction on the record.
Crosby said they fixed the credit on later pressings and 'evened things up with him with a whole mess of cash when the record went huge.' Rock and roll accounting, 1969 style.
Kantner's own band got its turn months later: Jefferson Airplane's version landed on Volunteers in November 1969, with slightly different lyrics.
CSN recorded their version on February 20, 1969, and made it the opening track of side two of their self-titled debut album, released May 29, 1969.
That debut album eventually went multi-platinum and was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame in 1999. Not bad for three guys from three broken bands.

title: Wooden Ships

description: Stephen Stills' alliteration-drunk farewell, sung in CSN's impossibly close three-part harmony. Just acoustic guitar and three voices from their 1969 debut album — under three minutes that launched a thousand harmony singers.

pops.text: Stephen Stills wrote this one alone, and it is a tongue-twister on purpose: 'Helplessly hoping her harlequin hovers nearby.' Count the H's.
Each verse line keys on a single letter — H, then G, then W: 'Gasping at glimpses of gentle true spirit,' 'Wordlessly watching he waits by the window.'
Stills later admitted, 'When I did the first few lines, I thought, How long can I keep this going?' His answer: the whole song. He also called it 'basically a country song.'
Stills credited his 10th-grade English teacher in Tampa, Florida: she got the football players to stand up and read poetry to impress her. 'Some of it must've rubbed off on me.'
The heartbreak underneath the wordplay was Judy Collins. Stills wrote it as their romance collapsed — the same breakup that fueled 'Suite: Judy Blue Eyes.'
The chorus does math and wordplay at once: 'They are one person, they are two alone, they are three together, they are for each other' — 'for' doubling as 'four.'
The singing mirrors the counting: the first line is sung solo, the second adds a voice, and by 'three together' all three are in. Harmony as arithmetic.
No drums, no bass, no band — just Stills' acoustic guitar and three voices, recorded at Wally Heider's Studio 3 in Hollywood for the trio's debut album.
CSN sang it at Woodstock in August 1969, in the acoustic set of what was only the band's second-ever live performance. No pressure, just half a million people.
The song keeps finding new rooms: it haunted the 2018 film Annihilation, and a 1969 Fillmore East live version headlined Rhino's Live At Fillmore East, 1969 album in 2024.

title: Helplessly Hoping

description: Seattle's Delvon Lamarr Organ Trio turns Tyrone Davis's soul plea into a sunny Hammond B-3 strut on their debut album Close But No Cigar. No singer, no problem — Lamarr's organ does all the begging, with Jimmy James on guitar.

pops.text: This is a cover — an instrumental remake of Tyrone Davis's soul classic, written by Barry Despenza and Carl Wolfolk. The trio lets the Hammond B-3 sing the vocal line.
Davis's original was almost an accident: it was the B-side of 'A Woman Needs to Be Loved' until radio DJs flipped the record over and made it the hit.
Flipped, it flew: Davis's version spent three weeks at No. 1 on Billboard's R&B chart, hit No. 5 on the Hot 100, and earned a gold disc for a million copies sold.
On February 1, 1969, Davis's single replaced Marvin Gaye's 'I Heard It Through the Grapevine' atop the R&B chart. Dethroning Marvin is a flex in any era.
The trio behind this version formed in Seattle in spring 2015, at the urging of Lamarr's wife Amy Novo — who became the band's manager. Every great organ trio needs a boss.
The debut lineup: Delvon Lamarr on Hammond B-3, Jimmy James on guitar, and David McGraw on drums. Three players, no bassist — Lamarr's feet and left hand cover the low end.
They started with a weekly residency at Seattle's Royal Room, woodshedding in public for a year before their debut album ever came out.
Colemine Records boss Terry Cole test-drove their tapes in his Ohio record shop; after watching 15 or 20 customers bob their heads and ask 'Who is this?', he signed on for the wide release.
Close But No Cigar was self-released in 2016, then reissued by Colemine in March 2018 — and topped Billboard's Contemporary Jazz Albums chart, hitting No. 3 on the Jazz Albums chart too.
Full circle: guitarist Jimmy James says when he and Lamarr first hung out, Lamarr quizzed him — 'Do you know Can I Change My Mind by Tyrone Davis?' He did. The band basically started there.

title: Can I Change My Mind

description: Title track of the Seattle trio's debut album — a greasy Hammond B-3 groove cut live in the studio, first self-released in 2016, then taken to No. 1 on Billboard's Contemporary Jazz Albums chart by Colemine Records.

pops.text: No singer, no problem: this is pure organ trio — Delvon Lamarr on Hammond B-3, Jimmy James on guitar and David McGraw on drums, talking to each other in groove.
The band behind it barely existed a year earlier. Lamarr's wife and manager Amy Novo founded the trio in Seattle in 2015 so he could focus on just writing and playing.
Lamarr started out as a drummer and trumpeter. Sitting in behind organist Joe Doria one night, he tried the Hammond — foot pedals and all — and, in his words, the organ chose him.
This is track 4 on the trio's debut album, also called Close But No Cigar — first self-released in 2016, then given a wide release by Colemine Records in March 2018.
The album was an accident. Engineer Jason Gray offered some free studio time, the band went in just to jam — and walked out with a debut album.
What you hear is basically live: the album was cut live in the studio to capture their club sound, with only a few tambourine overdubs added afterwards.
Critics hear Stax all over this title track — one review likens its melody to Jean Knight's 'Mr. Big Stuff,' with Lamarr stretching the chorus while the groove rolls on.
Colemine founder Terry Cole reportedly tested the tapes in his own record shop — after watching a roomful of customers bob their heads and ask who it was, he signed on.
The gamble paid off on the charts: the album hit No. 1 on Billboard's Contemporary Jazz Albums chart and No. 3 on the Jazz Albums chart.
The trio honed songs like this at a weekly residency at Seattle's Royal Room. Shazam clocks this one at a cool 103 beats per minute — proof you don't need speed to sweat.

title: Close but No Cigar

description: A two-minute-fifty-nine-second spy-soul strut from the Iowa City band's 2001 debut album Instrumental Action Soul — Hammond organ, clean guitar and pure B-movie intrigue, no words required.

pops.text: Iowa City, of all places: the Diplomats of Solid Sound dealt in Memphis-style soul and funk from the middle of Iowa corn country.
This is track 3 on their 2001 debut album, Instrumental Action Soul, released on the band's own Prescription Records.
The band began in 1998 as a side project of Iowa City retro-rockers the Bent Scepters — three Scepters teaming up with keyboardist Pat White.
When the Bent Scepters folded in 1999, the Diplomats carried on, and Nate 'Count' Basinger took over the Hammond organ chair — the engine of this sound.
'Willie's Theme' also did single duty in 2001, paired with 'Bullfrog Boogaloo' on a Prescription Records 7-inch from the band's first-single era.
The writing credit on this upload goes to guitarist Doug Roberson, while the producer credit goes to the whole band — solidarity, solid sound.
Their heroes are written all over the groove: reviewers name-check Booker T. & the MG's, the Meters and Hammond king Jimmy Smith as the band's holy trinity.
An album this cinematic was bound to travel: 'Willie's Theme' later surfaced on the Crime Jazz: Music to Spy By compilation — filed, perfectly, under 'Deleted Themes.'
The Freakonomics podcast became an unlikely fan, using Diplomats instrumentals — including cuts from this very album — as its between-segment music.
Two minutes fifty-nine seconds, zero lyrics. The Diplomats would add singers — the Diplomettes — in 2008, but this is the band in its original instrumental element.

title: Willie's Theme

description: Track 6 from Instrumental Action Soul (2001) — a five-minute Hammond-and-guitar workout, and a marathon by this band's standards, from an album that plays like a lost spy-movie soundtrack.

pops.text: Same album, longer leash: at five minutes, 'Chinese Connection' is a marathon next to the Diplomats' usual three-minute blasts — 'Willie's Theme' runs just 2:59.
It's track 6 of 13 on Instrumental Action Soul, the Iowa City band's 2001 debut on their own Prescription Records label.
The title shares its name with the American release title of Bruce Lee's Fist of Fury — fitting company on an album that closes with 'The Men From S.C.E.P.T.E.R. Theme.'
The Diplomats formed in 1998 as a side project of the Bent Scepters, an Iowa City band devoted to '60s garage rock — the soul thing was meant to be the side hustle.
Hammond organ drives everything here. The band's whole mission, per its AllMusic biography, was proving the mighty Hammond still had a place in 21st-century music.
Guitarist Doug Roberson has been at the band's core since the start — reviewers single out his big, clean guitar sound as the ground the organ dances on.
The recipe, per the critics: Booker T. & the MG's' strut, the Meters' funk and Jimmy Smith's B-3 fire, filtered through a Midwestern bar band's work ethic.
Garage-rock label Estrus Records liked what it heard: it put out a Diplomats single in the summer of 2002 and their second album, Let's Cool One, in 2003.
They took the show on the road, too: in the 2000s the Diplomats shared stages with Dick Dale, Alex Chilton and Blue Note organ legend Reuben Wilson.
Still instrumental, still grooving: the singers — the Diplomettes — didn't join until 2008, so this album remains the Diplomats in pure soundtrack mode.

title: Chinese Connection

description: Duran Duran's James Bond theme for Roger Moore's final 007 film — co-written with composer John Barry, it remains the only Bond theme ever to top the US Billboard Hot 100.

pops.text: Bond gets a theme, 1985-style: this is the title song from A View to a Kill, the 14th James Bond film — and Roger Moore's last outing as 007.

The band got the gig at a party. Bassist John Taylor, a lifelong Bond fan, asked producer Cubby Broccoli — after a few drinks — 'When are you going to get someone decent to do one of your theme songs?'
Broccoli called the bluff and paired them with Bond composer John Barry. Simon Le Bon later said Barry worked like a sixth member, sorting their good ideas from the bad ones.
Barry handled the arrangement and orchestra — the song was recorded in London with a 60-piece orchestra behind the band's synth-pop sheen.
Released 6 May 1985, it spent two weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 that July — still the only Bond theme ever to top the US chart.
The runners-up stopped short: Paul McCartney and Wings' 'Live and Let Die' and Carly Simon's 'Nobody Does It Better' both peaked at No. 2 in the US.
It earned a Golden Globe nomination for Best Original Song, too — not bad for a band that was quietly falling apart while it recorded the song.
The video, directed by Godley & Creme, edits the band into the film's Eiffel Tower action as spies — Nick Rhodes plays a fashion photographer, Andy Taylor a blind accordion player.
The timing was bittersweet: the band performed it at Live Aid in Philadelphia on 13 July 1985 — the day it hit No. 1 — in what became the original five's final performance together for years.
After John Barry died in 2011, Duran Duran closed their Coachella set with an orchestral version as a tribute — Le Bon back on stage in a tuxedo, Bond-style.

title: A View to a Kill

description: The Rio single that broke Duran Duran in America — a song written in an afternoon, a Sri Lanka adventure video and heavy MTV rotation turned it into a US No. 3 hit and a Grammy winner.

pops.text: That pulsing synth riff is Nick Rhodes, and the snarl over it is Andy Taylor's guitar — the song's two signature ingredients, produced by Colin Thurston for the album Rio.
Speed-writing, Duran-style: the song was reportedly written and recorded in a single Saturday afternoon in spring 1982, in the basement studios of EMI's London headquarters.
Released in the UK on 4 May 1982 as a single from Rio, it climbed to No. 5 at home — and helped push the album to No. 2 on the UK albums chart.
America wasn't buying — at first. The single flopped on its first US release in 1982, until producer David Kershenbaum remixed it, and Rio's first side, for American FM radio.
Then MTV did the rest: the channel put the video into heavy rotation, and the reissued single stormed to No. 3 on the Billboard Hot 100 in March 1983.
The video was a mini adventure movie: director Russell Mulcahy filmed the band on the hunt through the jungles and markets of Sri Lanka.
It made video history: in 1984, 'Hungry Like the Wolf' won the very first Grammy Award for Best Short Form Music Video.
Chart marathon: the song spent 23 weeks on the Hot 100 and hit No. 1 in Canada — a long way from its first, ignored American release.
It dragged the album up with it: Rio spent seven straight weeks at No. 6 in the US in spring 1983, as Duran Duran became leaders of the Second British Invasion.
The afterlife is secure: VH1 ranked it No. 3 on its 100 Greatest Songs of the '80s, and in 2021 Rolling Stone placed it at No. 398 on its 500 Greatest Songs of All Time.

title: Hungry Like the Wolf
